title: The Reader
author: Alexandre Dias
contentWarnings: Themes of loneliness and being unseen
excerpt: She had been reading Middlemarch when she found the first line. A small raised sentence on the soft skin just above her collarbone, in the small clean hand of what looked like faint sepia ink. She stared at it. It was, she recognized, her own thought.

chapters.title: The First Page
chapters.body:
She had been reading Middlemarch when she found the first line.

It was Tuesday evening. It was raining. She was in her small flat above the philosophy library, in the armchair by the window, with a cup of tea gone cold on the small table beside her and the copy of Middlemarch she had been meaning to reread for eleven years open on her lap. She had reached the passage where Dorothea, having married Casaubon, understood in a small terrible moment that she had married not a man but a folded set of intentions concerning her, and she had stopped reading, because the passage had reached her the way certain passages reached her, and she needed to sit with it before she went on.

She reached up, without looking, and rubbed absently at her collarbone.

Something was there.

She felt it before she saw it — a small raised line, thin as a hair, on the soft skin just above her right collarbone. She frowned. She lifted the neckline of her cardigan and looked down at her chest.

There was a sentence on her.

It was written in a small clean hand, in what looked like faint sepia ink, running for perhaps four centimeters just above her collarbone. She stared at it. She lifted the cardigan more. The sentence went on. It curved down over the front of her breast and continued along the underside, and she could not, from that angle, see how much further it went.

Miriam Ashe was forty-nine years old. She had been, for twenty-two years, a professor of Victorian literature at a small university in the north of England, and she had spent, by her own conservative estimate, some forty thousand hours reading. She had read Middlemarch six times. She had read The Mill on the Floss eight times, because her doctoral thesis had been on it. She had read every novel Trollope had ever published, and most of the letters, and had, in the course of her forty thousand hours, developed the particular capacity of the professional reader to hold in mind, with vivid specificity, whole paragraphs of prose she had absorbed once, ten or twenty years ago, and had thought never to think of again.

She knew the sentence on her collarbone.

She knew it because she had, at that exact moment, been reading it. Or rather, she had just finished reading it. The sentence on her collarbone was the sentence from Middlemarch that had, a minute earlier, made her stop.

It read: *she had married not a man but a folded set of intentions concerning her.*

Except it did not. That was not what George Eliot had written. That was what Miriam had thought when she had read it, the small internal paraphrase that had, in her reader's mind, resolved the passage down to its essence.

What was written on her collarbone was Miriam's own thought.

She sat in the armchair for a long time.

Middlemarch remained open on her lap. Her hand remained lifting the neckline of her cardigan. She stared down at the pale sepia writing on her chest, and she thought, with the specific coldness that came at the beginning of things she could not explain, that she must be mistaken.

She had a mole above her collarbone. She had had it since childhood. She was mistaking the mole. The rain, the low light of her single lamp, the strain of an hour's reading in poor light on old eyes — she was misperceiving what was actually a familiar bit of her own body.

She got up. She went to the bathroom. She turned on the light. She stood in front of the mirror and unbuttoned her cardigan to the waist and lifted her camisole.

She had a mole. It was where it had always been. Just below the mole, curving down toward her breast, was a sentence in her own thoughts, written on her, in ink that had not, as far as she could tell, come from anywhere.

She traced it with her finger. It did not smudge. She rubbed at it. It did not lift. She wet a flannel and scrubbed. Nothing.

She stood in the bathroom for a long time.

Eventually she buttoned her camisole. She buttoned her cardigan. She turned off the bathroom light and walked back into the sitting room, and she sat down in the armchair, and she looked at the open book on the small table where she had left it.

She had, she understood, three options. She could close the book, which would settle nothing. She could call someone, though she could not think whom. Or she could keep reading.

She picked up the book.

She kept reading.

—

By the end of the chapter there was a second sentence.

She had felt it happen this time. She had been reading a passage — a small aside where Eliot allowed herself an observation about the way certain kinds of intelligent women learned early to hide the reach of their intelligence from men whose reach was smaller, and how this hiding, done long enough, produced a woman who had forgotten she had once been reaching — and she had, upon finishing the passage, thought a specific thing about herself.

She had thought: *I did this. I have been doing this.*

And she had felt, in her right forearm, a small definite line of warmth. A stinging that was not exactly a stinging, more like the sensation of writing being pressed onto her from the inside.

She had put down the book. She had pushed up her sleeve.

*I did this. I have been doing this.*

The words ran along the inside of her forearm, from her elbow to her wrist, in the same small sepia hand as the first sentence. She sat and looked at them. She traced them with her fingertip. She was not, she noted, frightened. She was — she checked, honestly, because she was the sort of person who checked — very close to being frightened, but was not yet. What she was, in fact, was something more like recognized.

She thought: *of course. This is the shape of it.*

She had no idea what she meant by this. But she felt, when she thought it, that it was true.

—

She did not sleep well that night.

She did not sleep well because she kept getting up to check.

She had gone to bed at eleven, in her nightgown, with the light off and the rain still falling outside her window. She had lain very still. She had listened to her own breathing, which was, she noted, faster than usual. She had listened to the rain. She had tried, with the technique she had used since her twenties, to slow her breathing by counting.

She had reached seven, and had thought a thought, and had felt the small warmth on her ankle.

She had gotten up. She had turned on the bedside lamp. She had drawn back the covers and looked at her ankle.

*I have not been kind to my mother for many years.*

The sentence was on her ankle. In the same small sepia hand.

She sat on the edge of her bed.

The thought that had produced it — she could trace it back exactly. She had been counting her breaths and had thought, without meaning to, of her mother, of her mother's small careful voice on the telephone at Christmas, of the way her mother's voice had grown thin and hopeful over the last few years and how she, Miriam, had responded to the thinness and the hope by growing curter and more efficient in her replies. She had thought, in the seven-count of her breath, *I have not been kind to my mother for many years,* and she had rolled onto her side to sleep, and it had written itself on her ankle.

She had gotten up again at twelve-forty, and again at two-fifteen, and again at three-fifty, each time to a new thought recorded on a new part of her body. By four in the morning she had, running along her thigh, the sentence *I have wasted the last twenty years being frightened of the wrong things.* Along her collarbone had joined a second sentence: *I do not know when I stopped believing I would be loved.*

She stopped getting up.

She lay on her back in the dark. She could feel, faintly, the small heat of the newest line still cooling against her skin. She thought, and this thought too she felt inscribe itself, somewhere along her left flank where she could not see:

*This is not the first time this has happened to me.*

She was still for a long time.

She did not know why she had thought this. She had no memory of anything like this happening before. She was a woman who had lived a small careful life above a philosophy library in the north of England for twenty-two years, and if her body had ever behaved in this way she would, she thought, have remembered.

But she had thought it, and it had written itself, and she had not, in her whole life, learned to disbelieve the writing.

—

In the morning she cancelled her lectures for the week.

She sent one email to her department secretary, cited illness in the way that discouraged follow-up, and closed the browser. She sat at her small desk in her small flat, and she made a cup of tea, and she sat with the tea, and she thought about what she was going to do.

She was going to keep reading. That much was decided. She had made the decision the night before, at some level below thinking, in the seven-count of her breath, and she had felt the decision inscribe itself faintly along her ribs.

She was not going to go to a doctor. She had thought about this. She had rehearsed the visit. A woman of forty-nine walking into her GP's small surgery and lifting her shirt to reveal her own confessions written on her in sepia ink. She could imagine, with vivid clarity, the way the doctor would look at her. She could imagine the specialists. She could imagine the eventual diagnostic category — some new-named disorder of the skin combined with a psychiatric label, or a rare pigmentation disease, or a form of tactile hallucination she had somehow made real. She could imagine the treatment, whatever the treatment was, and she could imagine, above all, the sentences being *taken from her.*

She did not want the sentences taken from her.

This was, she understood as she thought it, the crux of it. Whatever was happening to her body was not, she had felt from the first sentence, an assault. It was more like a *transcription*. Something in her had begun, without her permission but without her opposition, to keep a record. And the record was — she looked down at her forearm — the record was of her own most honest thoughts. Thoughts she had had, apparently, for years, and had not, apparently, been recording.

She was not going to have the record taken from her.

She was going to read what was written.

She stood up. She went into the bathroom. She took off her clothes.

She stood in front of the small full-length mirror on the back of the bathroom door and she looked at herself.

She looked, she thought, small. She had never been a large woman, and had grown, over her forties, slightly smaller. Her body was not beautiful. It was not, on the other hand, unpleasant. It was the body of a woman who had lived quietly and eaten temperately and walked every day, a body that had been carefully unremarkable for a long time and had, in that unremarkableness, become almost invisible to her.

It was not invisible now.

Written on the pale skin of her chest and her forearms and her ankle and her thigh and, when she turned, on her lower back and along the outside of her left calf, were nine sentences. Nine confessions. Nine of her own most private thoughts, put down on her in the same small sepia hand, permanent and legible and hers.

She read them slowly.

She read them for a long time.

When she was done she pulled a chair from the kitchen into the sitting room, and she sat down in it in her dressing gown, and she picked up Middlemarch, and she began, on page one, to read again.

chapters.title: Chapter and Verse
chapters.body:
She read for eleven days.

She read Middlemarch through to the end, and she read Silas Marner, and she read The Mill on the Floss, and she read Daniel Deronda. She read The Portrait of a Lady, and Washington Square, and What Maisie Knew. She read Bleak House. She read Villette. She read every novel she had loved as a young woman, in the order in which she had first read them, at the pace at which she remembered reading them then, and she let her thoughts move as they moved and she let her body record what it recorded, and she did not, for eleven days, leave the flat.

By the third day she had run out of easily visible skin.

Her arms were covered — the inner forearms first, then the outer, then the backs of her hands. Her chest and belly were covered. Her thighs were covered, and her calves, and even the small ridges along the tops of her feet had, on the fifth day, begun to bear their small sentences. She had a mirror rigged, by then, on the back of her bedroom door, and each evening she took off her clothes and sat down on the bathroom stool and read what had been written that day.

The sentences were unsparing.

*I was afraid to have a child because I could not bear the idea of being loved by someone I could not disappoint.*

This one was written along her right ribs, curving with the shape of her.

*I have preferred books to people because books have never asked anything of me I could not give in silence.*

This one ran across her lower back.

*My father did not think I was clever. He thought my brother was clever. I have spent my adult life trying to prove him right about me and wrong about my brother.*

This one, the longest, ran from her left shoulder down her arm and across her wrist to her palm.

She read them each night. She did not weep over them. She had wept over things, in her life, but she had wept over things she had not yet quite understood, and these she understood too well to weep over. She read them the way she read the letters of Elizabeth Gaskell — with attention, with the small satisfaction of a hand recognized, with the strange comfort of finding out what had been said.

The comfort was, she had begun to see, the point.

She had spent forty-nine years thinking many thoughts and saying almost none of them aloud. She had spent her professional life reading other women's honest sentences and admiring them and teaching them and treating them as objects of study, and she had spent her private life keeping her own honest sentences small and quiet and folded into the interior of her days. She had a friend — she had one friend, a woman named Helen who worked in the medieval department and drank whisky on Fridays — to whom she said perhaps five per cent of what she thought. She had a mother to whom she said perhaps two per cent. She had, since her mid-thirties, said nothing of her actual life to anyone but the small silent audience of her own thinking.

And now, apparently, the audience had begun to write it down.

She sat on the bathroom stool on the sixth night and looked at the sentence *I have preferred books to people because books have never asked anything of me I could not give in silence,* and she thought, with a small clarity: *I have wanted, all my life, for someone to know this about me.*

She had not known, until she saw it written, that she had wanted this.

She wrote in a small notebook she had begun to keep — she had, from long habit, kept a notebook for every major reading project of her adult life — the following observation:

*What is written is what is confessed. What is confessed is what has been true.*

She read the sentence back. She thought about it. She added, on the next line:

*I have not, until this week, understood the word 'confession' to mean anything but a kind of guilty admission. It is beginning to mean, to me, something more like 'admission of what is already the case.'*

She underlined the last five words.

—

On the seventh day she noticed that new sentences had begun to appear in places she had not yet had any writing.

She had, until then, been receiving her sentences on the parts of her body that were, more or less, available for reading. Her arms. Her legs. Her torso. Her hands and feet. The undersides of her thighs, when she sat and looked. She had come to expect the writing to appear where she could find it.

On the seventh morning, when she stood in front of the bathroom mirror, she saw that there was writing on her scalp.

She parted her hair with two fingers, in the way she had parted her mother's hair as a small girl looking for grey. Written on her scalp, along the line where the skin was pale and had not seen the sun in decades, was a single sentence in the small sepia hand:

*I have not, since my grandmother's death, been touched by anyone in a way that was for me.*

She read the sentence twice.

She sat down on the bathroom stool with her legs pulled up under her, and she wrapped her arms around her knees, and she rested her forehead on her knees, and she stayed that way for perhaps half an hour.

She had not thought this thought. She was sure she had not thought this thought. She kept careful watch, now, of what she thought, because she wished to trace each new sentence back to its origin in her thinking — she had come to think of the process as *dictation*, and had begun to be able to feel a sentence being taken down, and to know within a minute or two what recent thought had produced it. And this sentence had not come from her recent thinking.

But it was true. She understood, as she sat with her forehead on her knees, that it was profoundly and precisely true. Since the death of her grandmother, when she had been twenty-two, no one had touched her the way her grandmother had touched her — with attention that had been about *her*, not about the other person's need to touch or be touched. She had had lovers. She had had a marriage that had ended after six years. She had had a mother who had held her arm, from time to time, in a way that had been meant to steady the mother. But no one, in twenty-seven years, had touched her in the way her grandmother had, and she had not, in twenty-seven years, allowed herself to notice that this was the case.

The sentence had noticed on her behalf.

She sat with the sentence for a long time. She understood, sitting with it, that whatever was writing on her was no longer confined to what she consciously thought. It had begun to write what she *knew* — what she carried but did not think — the deeper stratum of things she had, in the course of a life, believed but never once permitted to surface.

She got up. She went into the sitting room. She picked up Villette. She sat down.

She said, aloud, to no one, to the writing, to whatever was doing it:

*Go on. I am listening.*

She began to read.

—

By the ninth day the sentences had begun to touch each other.

She stood in front of the mirror on the ninth morning, and she saw that the sentences on her arms, which had until then been distinct — each running its own small course, separated by pale unmarked skin — had begun to grow toward each other. A line on the inside of her forearm reached down. A line on the outside of her wrist reached up. They met, on the seventh evening, at a place halfway between them, in a small careful serif, as if the two thoughts had recognized their kinship and had chosen to be, on her body, a single continuous sentence.

The combined sentence read:

*I have been afraid of being seen because being seen has always meant, in the end, being left; I have chosen to be alone rather than to survive that leaving again.*

She had not thought either of the halves, that morning, as a single thought. She had had two separate thoughts, separated by many hours. But the writing had linked them, and in the linking had produced a sentence that was — she read it twice — more true than either half alone.

She thought: *the writing is arranging me.*

She thought: *the writing is making me legible.*

She thought, with a small settled clarity: *I have been unreadable to myself for most of my life. This is being fixed.*

She looked at her body in the mirror. She was, she saw, becoming a text. Not metaphorically. Physically. The sentences on her had begun, over the last day, to organize into paragraphs, and the paragraphs had begun to compose a shape that was, she understood, a whole document. She could read it. She could sit down on the bathroom stool and read her own body from the wrist upward, from the ankle upward, and it made sense — it followed a coherent argument, it introduced its themes and developed them and complicated them.

The argument was: *this is who I am. This is who I have been.*

The document was, she understood, her own life.

The life had, at long last, gotten around to writing itself down.

—

On the eleventh day she was finished.

She had read the last of the novels she meant to reread. She had, that morning, finished A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man, which she had chosen last because it had been the book that had first made her want to be a scholar of literature, at nineteen, when she had understood for the first time that a book could be about the making of a person out of the words of that person, and that this was the specific thing she wanted to spend her life reading.

She had closed the book. She had stood up. She had gone into the bathroom.

She had taken off her nightgown, and she had stood in front of the mirror, and she had looked.

She was covered.

Every part of her that she could see and every part of her that she could reach was covered in the small sepia hand. Her arms. Her legs. Her chest and belly and back. Her scalp. Her face — she had, on the tenth day, begun to see writing on her cheeks and along her jawline, small sentences in a smaller hand. The soles of her feet had begun to bear their writing. Her palms. The tender skin of her eyelids, when she looked closely, had thin small lines running along their edges.

She was a book.

She stood in front of the mirror and she read what she could see of herself. She read for a long time. She read slowly, because it was longer than any of the novels she had spent the eleven days reading, because it was the argument and record of her entire interior life to the age of forty-nine, and because it was, in places, hard to read.

When she was done, she stood for a moment.

Then she turned. She looked over her shoulder, into the mirror, at her back.

There was, on her back, one final sentence.

It was written across her shoulder blades in a hand slightly larger than the rest, in ink slightly darker, and it was the only sentence on her that she had not, at any point in the last eleven days, thought.

It read:

*Someone must read what has been written.*

She stared at it.

She turned to face herself in the mirror. She looked at her covered body. She thought about what the sentence on her back was asking.

She had, she understood, been the writer, and now she needed to be read.

She began, slowly, to dress.

chapters.title: The Reader
chapters.body:
She went to Helen's flat on the twelfth day.

She had thought about who she could go to. She had thought about her mother, and had understood immediately that her mother could not be the one — her mother would call an ambulance, or a priest, or her own sister, or all three, and Miriam's body would be given to people who did not know how to read it. She had thought about her brother, and had discarded him for similar reasons. She had thought about her ex-husband, and had laughed once, softly, in the kitchen, because the notion was absurd.

She had come, at last, to Helen.

Helen was a medievalist. Helen had spent her career reading the marginalia of monks who had been dead for eight hundred years, and had learned, over that career, a certain patient attention to the specific voice of a specific hand. Helen would look at Miriam's body and would not, first, see a medical emergency. Helen would see, first, a text. Miriam knew this about Helen because she had spent twenty-two years with her.

She had put on a long coat, and boots, and a scarf pulled up over her chin, and she had walked the six streets to Helen's flat. It was late afternoon. It was still raining. She had walked with her hands deep in her pockets and her scarf close to her face, and no one had looked at her twice, because in the north of England in November no one looked at anyone twice.

She had rung Helen's bell.

Helen had come to the door in a jumper with a hole in one elbow, holding a glass of red wine.

Helen had looked at Miriam. Helen had said, immediately, without preamble: *Miriam. Where have you been.*

Miriam had said: *I need to show you something.*

Helen had stepped aside.

—

They went into Helen's small sitting room.

Miriam took off her coat. Her scarf. Her boots. She unbuttoned her cardigan and folded it over the back of a chair. She stood in the middle of Helen's small sitting room, in a plain camisole and a plain skirt, and she looked at Helen.

Helen had, at some point since answering the door, set down her wine.

Helen said, very quietly: *what.*

Miriam pulled up her sleeves.

Helen sat down in the small chair by the window. She did not say anything for a long time. She looked at Miriam's forearms — she could see, from where she sat, perhaps a fifth of what was written — and she looked at Miriam's face, and she looked back at the forearms.

At last she said: *sit down.*

Miriam sat down on the sofa opposite her.

Helen said: *may I read them?*

Miriam had, she realized, been afraid of this moment for eleven days without knowing she had been afraid. The thought of Helen reading what was written on her had been, in the back of Miriam's mind, an impossibility — the sentences were hers, they were her most private and most true, and to have them read by another person was to expose the whole interior of her to a witness. She had wanted a witness. She had also feared the witness with a fear so old it had become invisible to her, the same fear the writing had, on the ninth day, identified: *being seen has always meant, in the end, being left.*

She looked at Helen.

Helen was not going to leave. Helen had, over twenty-two years, given Miriam not a single sign of anything but patience. Helen had, in her way, been reading Miriam for two decades already. This was only the last, most literal, step of a long acquaintance.

Miriam said, quietly: *yes.*

Helen came and sat beside her on the sofa. Helen took Miriam's forearm in her two hands, gently, the way one might take an old book. She read.

She read the inside of the forearm. She turned it over and read the outside. She read the wrist. She took the other forearm and read it. She lifted, without ceremony, the hem of Miriam's camisole, and read what was on the belly. She read what was on the ribs. She said, once, softly, to a sentence Miriam could not see: *oh.*

She read for perhaps forty minutes.

When she was done, she sat back on the sofa, and she looked at Miriam. Her eyes were wet, but she was not crying.

She said: *this is what you have been thinking.*

Miriam said: *most of it. Some of it I did not know I had been thinking. But it is all true.*

Helen said: *for how long.*

Miriam said: *forever.*

They sat in the small sitting room in the rain in the north of England and looked at each other, and after a long while Helen took Miriam's hand — the hand with the writing on the palm — and held it in both of hers, and did not say anything more.

—

Miriam stayed at Helen's for four days.

She did not, for those four days, produce any more sentences. She had checked, several times, in Helen's bathroom mirror — she had looked at her scalp, at her face, at her arms — and there was nothing new. The last sentence, the one on her back, had been the last. The writing had, apparently, finished what it had come to write.

Helen had read all of it, over the four days, at Miriam's pace. Miriam had shown her what she could show. They had gone through the argument of Miriam's body in the way they might have gone through a long complicated poem in a graduate seminar — sitting together in the sitting room, reading aloud, pausing to discuss, taking coffee breaks. Helen had, at one point, brought out a magnifying glass to read the small sentences along Miriam's jaw. Miriam had read them aloud to her, because they were on her own face and she knew them without looking.

Helen had asked, on the second day: *what do you want to do.*

Miriam had said: *I don't know.*

Helen had said: *I mean, do you want to see anyone. A doctor. A —* she had paused, because she was the sort of scholar for whom the wrong word was worse than no word — *a priest.*

Miriam had said: *no.*

Helen had said: *what, then.*

Miriam had thought about it for a long time.

She had said, eventually: *I want to be able to be seen and to still be here afterward.*

Helen had said: *you are still here.*

Miriam had said: *I am still here.*

They had sat in the small kitchen with their tea.

Miriam had said: *what happens now?*

Helen had said: *I don't know. But I think — I think the writing is finished. And I think it has done what it came to do. And I think what you do next is up to you.*

Miriam had said: *what did it come to do?*

Helen had looked at her.

Helen had said: *it came to make you legible. It came to write down what you were carrying so you would not have to carry it in silence anymore. It came, I think, so that you could be *read.* So that someone could read you and know you and be here afterward.*

Miriam had said: *and now someone has.*

Helen had said: *yes.*

—

On the fifth morning Miriam went home to her small flat above the philosophy library.

She had, before leaving Helen's, gone into Helen's bathroom and looked at herself carefully in the mirror. She had, she thought, expected the sentences to have begun to fade. She had expected that once they had been read they might, having done their work, disappear.

They had not disappeared.

They were still there. All of them. In their small sepia hand. She could read them still, on her own body, in Helen's small bathroom on a Wednesday morning in November.

She had understood, standing in front of the mirror, that they were not going to disappear. That they had come to stay. That she was going to spend the rest of her life carrying, in her own skin, the whole recorded interior of a woman of forty-nine who had lived by silence for forty-nine years and had, at last, been transcribed.

She had thought: *I am going to have to dress carefully.*

She had thought: *I am going to have to keep some of this private.*

She had thought: *but I will know it is there.*

She had thought, with a small settled quietness: *I will know I have been read.*

—

She returned, that November, to the university.

She resumed her lectures. She wore, from then on, long sleeves and high collars, as she had always worn, and no one at the university had reason to suspect that anything had changed about her. Her lectures were, that term, slightly different. She spoke more slowly. She spoke, occasionally, of things she had not, in previous years, spoken of. She quoted, once, the sentence her body had produced about being seen and being left, though she attributed it to a nineteenth-century diarist she claimed to have been reading. Her students, some of them, wrote it down.

She had lunch with Helen every Friday. Helen did not, at these lunches, ask to read anything new. There was nothing new. They ate their sandwiches and drank their tea, and once or twice a term Helen would touch Miriam's forearm, briefly, as she passed her the salt, and the touch was different from any touch Miriam had had in twenty-seven years. It was the touch of someone who had read her.

Miriam grew old.

She died, in the end, at eighty-four, of a stroke in her sleep, in the same small flat above the philosophy library.

Helen had died four years before her, and it had been terrible, and Miriam had been the only one, at Helen's funeral, who had not entirely wept, because Miriam had had — for the first time in her life — the strange consolation of knowing that in dying, Helen had taken with her the reading of Miriam's body. Someone in the world had read what was written on her, and that someone was gone, and Miriam had gone on being a text without any current reader for four more years, and had understood, in those four years, that this too was all right. She had been read once. That was enough. It was, she had thought many times, sitting in her armchair, more than most people ever had.

She had left a note, in her desk, to be found after her death. The note had said:

*Please have my body cremated. Please do not permit any autopsy. I have spent a long life in ways I do not need to explain, and I ask this small last courtesy: that what is on me not be seen by strangers.*

The note had been honored.

Her body had been cremated. The sentences had gone with her.

No one, in the end, had read them except Helen. This too, Miriam had thought many times in her old age, was probably right. The writing had needed one reader. One reader was what it had asked for. One reader was what she had had. This was, she had come to think in her seventies, what most people meant by love — to be, in the whole length of a life, read by one person. Once. Fully. Without leaving.

She had been.

The rest, she thought, was extra.
